topics.title: Simple Machines (Inclined Plane): Meaning, Examples and Advantages of the Inclined Plane, and How to Make an Inclined Plane Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 4 Basic Science And Technology
topics.content:
SIMPLE MACHINES (INCLINED PLANE): MEANING, EXAMPLES AND ADVANTAGES OF INCLINED PLANE AND HOW TO MAKE AN INCLINED PLANE
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
PRIMARY 6 (BASIC 6) - THIRD TERM - WEEK 4
THEME - YOU AND ENERGY
PREVIOUS LESSON - Simple Machines (Pulley): Meaning, Examples, Types and Common Applications of Pulleys Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 3 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - SIMPLE MACHINES (INCLINED PLANE)
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning, Examples and Advantages of the Inclined Plane
3. How to Make an Inclined Plane
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define an inclined plane.
2. Identify examples of inclined planes.
3. State the advantages of an inclined plane.
4. Explain the uses of an inclined plane.
9. Construct a simple inclined plane using available materials.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned that simple machines make work easier. They also learned about levers and pulleys, which help people lift and move heavy objects.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing another simple machine called the inclined plane. Pupils will learn how a sloping surface helps people move heavy objects from one level to another with less effort.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Wooden board or cardboard
2. Books or blocks
3. Toy car
4. Small box
5. Ramp
6. Staircase
7. Pictures of ramps and slides
8. Charts showing inclined planes
9. Textbooks
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Have you ever seen a wheelchair being pushed up a ramp or a wheelbarrow being pushed up a sloping path? Have you walked up a staircase instead of climbing straight up? These are examples of an inclined plane.
An inclined plane is a sloping surface that helps people move heavy objects from one place to another with less effort. It is one of the six basic simple machines and is used in homes, schools, hospitals, markets, and construction sites.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of an inclined plane, examples, advantages, and how to make a simple inclined plane using everyday materials.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF AN INCLINED PLANE
An inclined plane is a sloping or slanting surface that helps people move heavy objects from one level to another with less effort.
It is one of the six basic simple machines.
Examples of an Inclined Plane
1. Ramp
2. Staircase
3. Slide in a playground
4. Sloping road
5. Loading ramp for trucks
6. Wheelchair ramp
ADVANTAGES OF AN INCLINED PLANE
1. It makes work easier.
2. It reduces the effort needed to move heavy objects.
3. It helps move loads safely from one level to another.
4. It saves time and energy.
5. It makes it easier for people using wheelchairs to move.
6. It is useful in homes, schools, hospitals, markets, and construction sites.
LESSON 2 - USES OF AN INCLINED PLANE
1. Moving goods into trucks.
2. Helping wheelchair users enter buildings.
3. Walking up staircases.
4. Sliding down playground slides.
5. Moving heavy loads to higher places.
LESSON 3 - HOW TO MAKE AN INCLINED PLANE
Materials Needed:
- A wooden board or thick cardboard
- Two or three books or blocks
- A toy car or small box
Procedure
1. Place the books or blocks on a flat table.
2. Lean one end of the wooden board or cardboard on the books.
3. Leave the other end resting on the table or floor.
4. Place the toy car or small box at the lower end of the board.
5. Push the toy car or box gently up the sloping board.
6. Observe how the object moves up the slope with less effort.
Observation:
- The sloping board forms an inclined plane.
- It is easier to push the object up the slope than to lift it straight up.
Conclusion: An inclined plane is a simple machine that makes it easier to move heavy objects from one level to another by using a sloping surface. It reduces the effort needed to do work.
Safety Precautions
1. Use light objects during the activity.
2. Place the inclined plane on a stable surface.
3. Do not push objects too fast.
4. Keep the activity area clean and free from obstacles.
5. Work under the teacher’s supervision.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. An inclined plane is a ______.
A. wheel
B. sloping surface
C. rope
D. screw
2. An inclined plane is used to ______.
A. move heavy objects with less effort
B. make work harder
C. produce electricity
D. measure weight
3. Which of the following is an example of an inclined plane?
A. Ramp
B. Hammer
C. Pulley
D. Knife
4. Which of the following is used by wheelchair users?
A. Staircase
B. Crowbar
C. Spade
D. Ramp
5. Which of the following is NOT an inclined plane?
A. Slide
B. Sloping road
C. Bottle opener
D. Staircase
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. An inclined plane is a ______ surface.
7. A ______ helps people move heavy loads into a truck.
8. An inclined plane reduces the ______ needed to move heavy objects.
9. A ______ is found in many playgrounds.
10. An inclined plane is one of the ______ simple machines.
C. True or False
11. An inclined plane makes work easier. ______
12. A staircase is an inclined plane. ______
13. An inclined plane increases the effort needed to do work. ______
14. A ramp is an example of an inclined plane. ______
15. An inclined plane can be made with a wooden board and books. ______
D. Match Column A with Column B
Column A - Column B
16. Ramp - A. Playground equipment
17. Slide - B. Used by wheelchair users
18. Staircase - C. Used to move between floors
19. Loading ramp - D. Used to load goods into trucks
20. Inclined Plane - E. A sloping simple machine
ANSWER KEYS
1. B - Sloping surface
2. A - Move heavy objects with less effort
3. A - Ramp
4. D - Ramp
5. C - Bottle opener
6. Sloping
7. Loading ramp
8. Effort
9. Slide
10. Six
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. True
16. B - Ramp → Used by wheelchair users
17. A - Slide → Playground equipment
18. C - Staircase → Used to move between floors
19. D - Loading ramp → Used to load goods into trucks
20. E - Inclined plane → A sloping simple machine
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that an inclined plane is a sloping surface that helps people move heavy objects from one level to another with less effort. They learned that an inclined plane is one of the six basic simple machines.
Pupils identified common examples of inclined planes, including ramps, staircases, slides, sloping roads, loading ramps, and wheelchair ramps.
They also learned the advantages of an inclined plane, such as making work easier, reducing effort, saving time and energy, helping people move heavy loads safely, and making buildings more accessible for wheelchair users.
Finally, pupils learned how to make a simple inclined plane by placing one end of a wooden board or cardboard on books or blocks to form a sloping surface. They observed that it is easier to push an object up the slope than to lift it straight up.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays pictures or real examples of inclined planes such as a ramp, staircase, slide, and loading ramp.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and identify the inclined planes.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of an inclined plane.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define an inclined plane in their own words.
3. The teacher discusses the examples and advantages of an inclined plane.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of inclined planes and state their advantages.
4. The teacher demonstrates how to make a simple inclined plane using a wooden board and books.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and use the inclined plane to move a toy car or small box.
5. The teacher explains the uses of inclined planes in homes, schools, hospitals, and construction sites.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify places where inclined planes are used in their community.
6. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively in the discussion.
7. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and write the key points in their notebooks.
8. The teacher gives classwork, marks pupils’ responses, and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Forces: Meaning and Examples of Force (Push and Pull), Evidence and Effects of Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 5 Basic Science and Technology
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is an inclined plane?
2. Mention five examples of an inclined plane.
3. State five advantages of an inclined plane.
4. Explain how an inclined plane makes work easier.
5. Mention four uses of an inclined plane in everyday life.
6. Describe how to make a simple inclined plane using available materials.
7. Why is a ramp considered an inclined plane?
8. State two safety precautions to observe when making and using a simple inclined plane.

topics.title: Forces: Meaning and Examples of Force (Push and Pull), Evidence and Effects of Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 5 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
FORCES: MEANING AND EXAMPLES OF FORCE (PUSH AND PULL), EVIDENCE AND EFFECTS OF FORCE
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
PRIMARY 6 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - LEARNING ABOUT OUR ENVIRONMENT
PREVIOUS LESSON - Simple Machines (Inclined Plane): Meaning, Examples and Advantages of the Inclined Plane, and How to Make an Inclined Plane Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 4 Basic Science And Technology
TOPIC - FORCES (PUSH AND PULL)
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Examples of Force (Push and Pull)
3. Evidence and Effects of Force
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define force.
2. Explain the meaning of push and pull as examples of force.
3. Identify examples of force in everyday life.
4. State the evidence of force.
5. Explain the effects of force on objects.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about simple machines such as levers, pulleys, and inclined planes. They know that these machines make work easier by helping people lift, move, or carry objects.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing force, which is the push or pull used to move or stop objects. Pupils will learn that force is needed for simple machines and for many everyday activities.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Football
2. Toy car
3. Rope
4. Spring
5. Door
6. Wheelbarrow
7. Charts showing push and pull activities
8. Textbooks
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every day, we push and pull different objects. We push a door to open it, pull a bucket from a well, kick a football, or pull a chair closer to us. These actions involve force.
Force helps objects move, stop, change direction, or change shape. Without force, many of our daily activities would not be possible.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of force, examples of force (push and pull), the evidence of force, and the effects of force on objects.
MEANING OF FORCE
A force is a push or a pull applied to an object. Force is needed to move, stop, lift, or change the direction of an object.
Force helps us carry out many activities every day.
EXAMPLES OF FORCE
There are two main examples of force:
1. Push
A push is a force used to move an object away from you.
Examples of Push:
- Pushing a door to open it.
- Pushing a shopping trolley.
- Pushing a wheelbarrow.
- Pushing a toy car.
- Kicking a football.
- Pushing a table.
2. Pull
A pull is a force used to bring an object towards you.
Examples of Pull:
- Pulling a door to close or open it.
- Pulling a bucket from a well.
- Pulling a drawer.
- Pulling a rope.
- Pulling a suitcase.
- Pulling a chair closer.
DIFFERENCES BETWEEN PUSH AND PULL
1. A push moves an object away from you, while a pull brings an object towards you.
2. A push is used to open a door by pushing it, while a pull is used to open or close a door by pulling it.
3. A push moves an object forward, while a pull brings an object closer.
EVIDENCE OF FORCE
We know that a force is acting when we observe any of the following:
1. An object starts moving.
2. A moving object stops.
3. An object changes direction.
4. An object changes speed.
5. An object changes its shape or size.
EFFECTS OF FORCE
Force can produce the following effects:
1. Force can move a stationary object.
- Example: Pushing a toy car makes it move.
2. Force can stop a moving object.
- Example: Catching a moving ball stops it.
3. Force can change the direction of an object.
- Example: Hitting a football changes its direction.
4. Force can change the speed of an object.
- Example: Pedalling a bicycle faster increases its speed.
5. Force can change the shape of an object.
- Example: Squeezing a sponge or stretching a rubber band changes its shape.
6. Force can lift or lower an object.
- Example: Lifting a school bag from the floor.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Force is a ________.
A. colour
B. machine
C. shape
D. push or pull
2. Which of the following is an example of a push?
A. Pulling a drawer
B. Pulling a bucket from a well
C. Pushing a wheelbarrow
D. Pulling a rope
3. Which of the following is an example of a pull?
A. Pushing a shopping trolley
B. Kicking a football
C. Pulling a suitcase
D. Pushing a table
4. Which of the following is an effect of force?
A. It can move an object.
B. It changes the colour of an object.
C. It makes an object disappear.
D. It changes the weather.
5. Which of the following shows evidence of force?
A. An object changes direction.
B. An object remains in the same position.
C. A book remains on a table.
D. A chair remains still.
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. A force is a __________ or a __________.
7. A __________ moves an object away from you.
8. A __________ brings an object towards you.
9. Force can change the __________ of an object.
10. Force can change the __________ of an object.
C. True or False
11. Force can stop a moving object. ______
12. Pulling a rope is an example of a push. ______
13. A force can change the direction of an object. ______
14. Kicking a football is an example of applying force. ______
15. Force cannot change the shape of an object. ______
D. Match Column A with Column B
Column A - Column B
16. Push - A. Brings an object towards you
17. Pull - B. Moves an object away from you
18. Kicking a football - C. Changes the direction of the ball
19. Squeezing a sponge - D. Stops the ball
20. Catching a moving ball - E. Changes the shape of the sponge
ANSWER KEYS
1. D - Push or pull
2. C - Pushing a wheelbarrow
3. C - Pulling a suitcase
4. A - It can move an object.
5. A - An object changes direction.
6. Push, pull
7. Push
8. Pull
9. Direction
10. Shape
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. True
15. False
16. B - Push → Moves an object away from you
17. A - Pull → Brings an object towards you
18. C - Kicking a football → Changes the direction of the ball
19. E - Squeezing a sponge → Changes the shape of the sponge
20. D - Catching a moving ball → Stops the ball
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that force is a push or a pull applied to an object. They learned that force is needed to move, stop, lift, or change the direction of an object.
Pupils identified the two main examples of force:
- Push - moves an object away from a person.
- Pull - brings an object towards a person.
They also learned the evidence of force, which includes an object starting to move, stopping, changing direction, changing speed, or changing shape.
Finally, pupils learned the effects of force, such as moving a stationary object, stopping a moving object, changing the direction or speed of an object, changing the shape of an object, and lifting or lowering objects. They concluded that force is used in many everyday activities and is important in carrying out work efficiently.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays objects such as a ball, toy car, rope, door, and wheelbarrow and demonstrates pushing and pulling them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and identify actions that involve pushing and pulling.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of force as a push or a pull.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define force in their own words.
3. The teacher explains the examples of force (push and pull) using familiar classroom and home activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of push and pull from their daily lives.
4. The teacher explains the evidence of force, showing how force can make objects move, stop, change direction, change speed, or change shape.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and identify the evidence of force during the demonstration.
5. The teacher discusses the effects of force on objects using practical examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the different effects of force and give examples.
6. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively in the discussion.
7. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and write the key points in their notebooks.
8. The teacher gives classwork, marks pupils’ responses, and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Forces: Meaning and Examples of Force (Push and Pull), Evidence and Effects of Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 5 Basic Science and Technology
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is force?
2. State the two main examples of force.
3. Explain the difference between a push and a pull.
4. Mention five examples of push and pull in everyday life.
5. State five pieces of evidence that show a force is acting on an object.
6. Mention five effects of force on objects.
7. Explain how force is used in our daily activities.
8. Demonstrate one example each of a push and a pull using objects in the classroom.

topics.title: Forces: Meaning and Effects of Frictional Force, Advantages and Disadvantages of Frictional Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 6 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
FORCES: MEANING AND EFFECTS OF FRICTIONAL FORCE, ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF FRICTIONAL FORCE
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
PRIMARY 6 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 6
THEME - LEARNING ABOUT OUR ENVIRONMENT
PREVIOUS LESSON - Forces: Meaning and Examples of Force (Push and Pull), Evidence and Effects of Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 5 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - FRICTIONAL FORCE
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Effects of Frictional Force
3. Advantages and Disadvantages of Frictional Force
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define frictional force.
2. Explain the effects of frictional force.
3. State the advantages of frictional force.
4. State the disadvantages of frictional force.
5. Identify everyday activities where friction is useful or harmful.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned that force is a push or a pull used to move, stop, or change the direction of an object. They also learned that force has different effects on objects.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing frictional force, which is a type of force that acts when two surfaces touch and opposes their movement. Pupils will learn how friction affects everyday activities and why it can be both useful and harmful.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Wooden block
2. Sandpaper
3. Smooth plastic surface
4. Toy car
5. Football
6. Shoe
7. Bicycle brake
8. Eraser
9. Charts showing examples of friction
10. Textbooks
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Have you ever tried to push a heavy table across the floor? Have you noticed that a bicycle stops when the brakes are applied, or that you do not slip easily while walking? These activities happen because of frictional force.
Frictional force acts between two surfaces that are in contact. It helps us walk safely, write with a pencil, and stop moving vehicles. However, it can also cause wear and tear on machine parts and make movement more difficult.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of frictional force, its effects, and the advantages and disadvantages of friction in everyday life.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF FRICTIONAL FORCE
Frictional force is the force that opposes or resists the movement of one object over another when their surfaces are in contact.
Friction slows down or prevents objects from moving easily.
EFFECTS OF FRICTIONAL FORCE
Frictional force has the following effects:
1. It slows down moving objects.
- Example: A bicycle slows down when the brakes are applied.
2. It stops moving objects.
- Example: A rolling football eventually stops because of friction with the ground.
3. It makes walking possible without slipping.
- Example: Friction between shoes and the ground helps us walk safely.
4. It produces heat.
- Example: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm.
5. It causes wear and tear.
- Example: The soles of shoes and vehicle tyres wear out after long use.
6. It makes writing possible.
- Example: Friction between a pencil and paper allows us to write.
7. It can make movement more difficult.
- Example: It takes more effort to push a heavy box across a rough floor than a smooth floor.
LESSON 2 - ADVANTAGES OF FRICTIONAL FORCE
Friction is useful in many ways. Some advantages include:
1. It helps us walk and run without slipping.
2. It helps vehicles stop when brakes are applied.
3. It makes writing on paper possible.
4. It helps us hold or grip objects firmly.
5. It prevents objects from sliding easily.
6. It helps nails, screws, and bolts stay firmly in place.
DISADVANTAGES OF FRICTIONAL FORCE
Although friction is useful, it also has some disadvantages:
1. It causes wear and tear of machine parts, tyres, and shoe soles.
2. It produces unwanted heat in machines.
3. It slows down the movement of objects.
4. It wastes energy because more effort is needed to move objects.
5. It can damage machine parts if not properly lubricated.
6. It increases the cost of maintaining machines due to repairs and replacement of worn parts.
REDUCING FRICTION
Friction can be reduced by:
1. Applying oil or grease to machine parts.
2. Using wheels or rollers.
3. Polishing rough surfaces.
4. Using ball bearings in machines.
LESSON 3 - WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Frictional force is a force that ______.
A. attracts objects
B. opposes movement between two surfaces
C. produces electricity
D. changes colour
2. Which of the following is an advantage of friction?
A. It causes wear and tear.
B. It wastes energy.
C. It damages machines.
D. It helps us walk without slipping.
3. Which of the following is a disadvantage of friction?
A. It helps us write.
B. It helps vehicles stop.
C. It causes wear and tear of tyres.
D. It helps us hold objects.
4. Which of the following can reduce friction?
A. Oil or grease
B. Sand
C. Water only
D. Stones
5. Friction produces ______.
A. Rain
B. Heat
C. Wind
D. Light
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. Frictional force ______ the movement of objects.
7. Friction helps us ______ without slipping.
8..Oil and grease are used to ______ friction.
9. Friction produces ______ when two surfaces rub together.
10. Friction causes ______ and tear of machine parts.
C. True or False
11. Friction helps vehicles stop safely. ______
12. Friction makes writing on paper possible. ______
13. Friction never causes damage to machines. ______
14. Lubrication helps to reduce friction. ______
15. Friction always makes movement easier. ______
D. Match Column A with Column B
Column A - Column B
16. Walking - A. Opposes movement
17. Brakes - B. Helps us stop vehicles
18. Rubbing hands together - C. Reduces friction
19. Oil or grease - D. Helps us walk without slipping
20. Friction - E. Produces heat
ANSWER KEYS
1. B
2. D
3. C
4. A
5. B
6. Opposes
7. Walk
8. Reduce
9. Heat
10. Wear
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. False
16. D - Walking → Helps us walk without slipping
17. B - Brakes → Helps us stop vehicles
18. E - Rubbing hands together → Produces heat
19. C - Oil or grease → Reduces friction
20. A - Friction → Opposes movement
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that frictional force is the force that opposes or resists the movement of objects when two surfaces are in contact. They learned that friction affects many activities in everyday life.
Pupils identified the effects of frictional force, such as slowing down or stopping moving objects, changing the speed of objects, producing heat, causing wear and tear, making walking and writing possible, and making movement more difficult.
They also learned the advantages of friction, including helping people walk without slipping, allowing vehicles to stop safely, making writing possible, helping people grip objects firmly, and preventing objects from sliding.
Finally, pupils learned the disadvantages of friction, such as causing wear and tear of machine parts and tyres, producing unwanted heat, slowing movement, wasting energy, and increasing the cost of maintaining machines. They concluded that friction is both useful and harmful, and that lubrication and the use of rollers or ball bearings can help reduce unwanted friction.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays objects such as a wooden block, sandpaper, smooth plastic surface, toy car, shoe, bicycle brake, and eraser.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the objects and identify situations where friction occurs.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of frictional force and demonstrates rubbing two surfaces together.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain frictional force in their own words and observe the demonstration.
3. The teacher discusses the effects of frictional force using practical examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and explain the effects of friction they observe.
4. The teacher explains the advantages of frictional force with examples from daily life.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention activities where friction is useful.
5. The teacher explains the disadvantages of frictional force and demonstrates how oil or grease reduces friction.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify situations where friction is harmful and suggest ways of reducing it.
6. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively in the discussion.
7. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and write the key points in their notebooks.
8. The teacher gives classwork, marks pupils’ responses, and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

3. State five advantages of frictional force.
4. State five disadvantages of frictional force.
5. Mention four everyday activities where friction is useful.
6. Mention three ways of reducing friction.
7. Explain why oil or grease is applied to machine parts.
8. State the difference between the advantages and disadvantages of frictional force.

topics.content:
WATER PROJECT: MEANING AND EXAMPLES WATER PROJECT IN NIGERIA, BENEFITS AND HAZARDS OF WATER PROJECTS
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
PRIMARY 6 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 8
THEME - YOU AND ENERGY
PREVIOUS LESSON - Forces: Meaning and Effects of Frictional Force, Advantages and Disadvantages of Frictional Force Primary 6 (Basic 6) Third Term Week 6 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - WATER PROJECT IN NIGERIA
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Examples of Water Projects in Nigeria
3. Benefits and Hazards of Water Projects
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define water projects.
2. Identify examples of water projects in Nigeria.
3. State the benefits of water projects.
4. Explain the hazards of water projects.
5. Appreciate the importance of water projects in community development.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about water, its sources, uses, and the importance of clean water for healthy living. They know that water is needed for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, and other daily activities.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing water projects, which are facilities developed to provide, store, treat, and distribute clean water to homes, schools, industries, farms, and communities. Pupils will also learn about the benefits and hazards of these water projects.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of dams, boreholes, wells, and water treatment plants
2. Chart showing water projects
3. Map of Nigeria
4. Textbooks
5. Clean water samples (if available)
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Clean water is needed for good health and development. To ensure that people have enough safe water, governments and communities build different water projects such as dams, boreholes, and water treatment plants.
These projects supply water for homes, schools, hospitals, industries, and farms. However, while water projects have many benefits, they can also create some challenges if they are not properly planned or managed.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of water projects, examples of water projects in Nigeria, as well as their benefits and hazards.
MEANING OF WATER PROJECTS
Water projects are facilities or programmes built to provide, store, treat, or distribute clean and safe water for people, farms, industries, and communities.
Water projects help to ensure that people have enough water for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, and other daily activities.
EXAMPLES OF WATER PROJECTS IN NIGERIA
1. Boreholes - Deep holes drilled into the ground to obtain clean underground water.
2. Wells - Water sources dug into the ground for domestic use.
3. Dams - Large structures built across rivers to store water for homes, farming, electricity generation, and flood control.
4. Water Treatment Plants - Facilities where dirty water is treated to make it safe for drinking.
5. Water Supply Schemes - Projects that distribute clean water through pipes to homes, schools, hospitals, and communities.
6. Overhead Water Tanks - Large tanks used to store and supply water to buildings and communities.
EXAMPLES OF MAJOR WATER PROJECTS IN NIGERIA
1. Kainji Dam - Niger State.
2. Shiroro Dam - Niger State.
3. Jebba Dam - Kwara/Niger States.
4. Ikere Gorge Dam - Oyo State.
5. Challawa Gorge Dam - Kano State.
IMPORTANCE OF WATER PROJECTS
1. They provide clean and safe water.
2. They support farming through irrigation.
3. They supply water for industries and businesses.
4. Some dams generate electricity.
5. They improve the health and well-being of communities.
Water projects are facilities developed to provide, store, treat, and distribute clean water. Examples include boreholes, wells, dams, water treatment plants, water supply schemes, and overhead water tanks. Major water projects in Nigeria include Kainji Dam, Shiroro Dam, Jebba Dam, Ikere Gorge Dam, and Challawa Gorge Dam.
BENEFITS OF WATER PROJECTS
Water projects are important because they improve the lives of people and support national development. Their benefits include:
1. They provide clean and safe water for drinking and cooking.
2. They improve public health by reducing water-borne diseases.
3. They supply water for farming and irrigation.
4. They provide water for industries and businesses.
5. Some dams generate electricity for homes and industries.
6. They create employment opportunities during construction and maintenance.
7. They improve sanitation and hygiene in communities.
8. They support fishing, recreation, and tourism in some areas.
HAZARDS OF WATER PROJECTS
Although water projects are beneficial, they can also have some negative effects if not properly managed. These include:
1. Flooding when dams overflow or collapse.
2. Displacement of people from their homes during the construction of dams.
3. Loss of farmland and vegetation.
4. Water pollution if water sources are not properly protected.
5. Spread of water-related diseases when water becomes stagnant.
6. Accidents such as drowning in dams, rivers, or reservoirs.
7. High cost of constructing and maintaining water projects.
8. Damage to the environment if projects are poorly planned.
SAFETY MEASURES AROUND WATER PROJECTS
1. Do not swim in dams or reservoirs without permission.
2. Keep water sources clean and free from waste.
3. Obey warning signs around water projects.
4. Report leaking pipes or damaged water facilities.
5. Avoid playing near deep water bodies.
Water projects provide many benefits, such as supplying clean water, improving health, supporting farming, generating electricity, creating jobs, and promoting development. However, they also have hazards, including flooding, displacement of people, water pollution, drowning, and environmental damage. Proper planning, maintenance, and safety practices help reduce these hazards.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Water projects are developed to ______.
A. provide clean and safe water
B. destroy rivers
C. pollute water
D. reduce rainfall
2. Which of the following is a water project?
A. Market
B. Stadium
C. Airport
D. Borehole
3. Which of the following is a major dam in Nigeria?
A. Kainji Dam
B. Zuma Rock
C. National Theatre
D. Tafawa Balewa Square
4. Which of the following is a benefit of water projects?
A. Water pollution
B. Flooding
C. Supply of clean water
D. Deforestation
5. Which of the following is a hazard of water projects?
A. Provision of irrigation water
B. Flooding
C. Generation of electricity
D. Improved sanitation
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. Water projects provide ______ and safe water.
7. A ______ is a deep hole drilled into the ground to obtain water.
8. ______ plants treat dirty water to make it safe for drinking.
9. One major water project in Niger State is ______ Dam.
10. Flooding is one ______ of water projects.
C. True or False
11. Boreholes are examples of water projects. ______
12. Water projects help improve public health. ______
13. Water projects cannot be used for irrigation. ______
14. Drowning can occur around dams and reservoirs. ______
15. Water projects have only benefits and no hazards. ______
D. Match Column A with Column B
Column A - Column B
16. Borehole - A. Hazard of water projects
17. Dam - B. Helps farmers grow crops
18. Water treatment plant - C. Makes dirty water safe for drinking
19. Flooding - D. Generates electricity and stores water
20. Irrigation - E. Supplies underground water
ANSWER KEYS
1. A - Provide clean and safe water
2. D - Borehole
3. A - Kainji Dam
4. C - Supply of clean water
5. B - Flooding
6. Clean
7. Borehole
8. Water treatment
9. Kainji
10. Hazard
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. False
16. E - Borehole → Supplies underground water
17. D - Dam → Generates electricity and stores water
18. C - Water treatment plant → Makes dirty water safe for drinking
19. A - Flooding → Hazard of water projects
20. B - Irrigation → Helps farmers grow crops
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that water projects are facilities or programmes developed to provide, store, treat, and distribute clean and safe water for homes, schools, farms, industries, and communities.
They identified examples of water projects in Nigeria, such as boreholes, wells, dams, water treatment plants, water supply schemes, and overhead water tanks. They also learned about major dams in Nigeria, including Kainji Dam, Shiroro Dam, Jebba Dam, Ikere Gorge Dam, and Challawa Gorge Dam.
Pupils discussed the benefits of water projects, including the provision of clean water, improved public health, support for farming through irrigation, generation of electricity, creation of employment opportunities, and improvement of sanitation.
Finally, they learned the hazards of water projects, such as flooding, displacement of people, water pollution, drowning, spread of water-related diseases, and environmental damage. They concluded that water projects are important for national development but must be properly managed and used safely to reduce their hazards.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays pictures or charts of boreholes, wells, dams, water treatment plants, overhead water tanks, and major dams in Nigeria.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and identify the different water projects.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of water projects.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define water projects in their own words.
3. The teacher discusses examples of water projects in Nigeria and their locations.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of water projects found in their communities and in Nigeria.
4. The teacher explains the benefits of water projects with practical examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and explain the benefits of water projects to individuals and communities.
5. The teacher discusses the hazards of water projects and explains safety measures around dams, rivers, and reservoirs.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the hazards of water projects and suggest ways to stay safe around water bodies.
6. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively in the discussion.
7. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and write the key points in their notebooks.
8. The teacher gives classwork, marks pupils’ responses, and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON

LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What are water projects?
2. Mention five examples of water projects in Nigeria.
3. Name three major dams in Nigeria.
4. State five benefits of water projects.
5. Mention five hazards of water projects.
6. Explain why water treatment plants are important.
7. State four safety measures to observe around water projects.
8. Explain why water projects are important for the development of communities and the nation.
